en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga,
Pārājika Section
7. The Training Rule on Following One Who Has Been Suspended At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā was associating with the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha—who had formerly been a vulture-trainer—and who had been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha.
Those bhikkhunīs who were few in desires … [as before] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the noble lady Thullanandā comply with the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-trainer, who has been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, bhikkhus, that the bhikkhunī Thullanandā complies with the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-trainer, who has been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha?”
“It is true, Blessed One,” they replied.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can this be, monks? How indeed can the nun Thullanandā follow the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-keeper, who has been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence … [and so forth] … And thus,
monks, the nuns should recite this training rule: ‘Whatever nun, however,
[should associate with] a monk who has been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction …’”
If she should continue to follow that monk who is disrespectful, unrepentant, and has not made amends, that bhikkhunī should be addressed by the bhikkhunīs thus:

“Venerable lady, this monk has been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction; he is disrespectful, unrepentant, and has not made amends. Venerable lady, do not follow this monk.

If, even when addressed by the bhikkhunīs in this way, that bhikkhunī persists as before, that bhikkhunī is to be formally admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that course of action.
"If, even after being admonished up to three times, she should relinquish it, that is well;
but if she does not relinquish it, she too is one who has committed a *pārājika* offense, one who is no longer in communion, and one who follows the suspended. As for the words "But she who":
Whichever [nun] of such a kind... "bhikkhunī" ...pe...
this is the nun intended in this context.
A "unified" Saṅgha is one that shares the same residence and stands within the same boundary.
A "suspended" [person] is one...
One who has been suspended for not seeing an offense, or for not making amends for it,
or for not relinquishing it. "In accordance with the Dhamma and the Vinaya" means by whichever Dhamma and by whichever Vinaya.
"By the Teacher's instruction" means by the Victor’s instruction, by the Buddha’s instruction.
"Lack of respect" means:
He does not acknowledge the Saṅgha, the group, the individual, or the formal act. One who does not make amends is one who has been suspended and not reinstated.
"Those who have not made companions" means that monks who share the same communal residence are called "companions.
He has none such with him; therefore, he is called "one who has not made companions."
"She would conform to his views" means:
whatever view he has, whatever inclination he has, whatever preference he has, she too would have that same view, that same inclination, and that same preference.
"That nun" refers to her.
Regarding that nun who follows one who has been suspended:
"By the nuns" means by other nuns. Those who see her or hear of her should say to her:

“Venerable lady, this bhikkhu has indeed been expelled by a unanimous Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction; he is disrespectful, unrepentant, and has not made amends.
Venerable lady, do not follow after this bhikkhu.
This should be said a second time as well.
A third time she should be told.
If she relinquishes it, that is well;
if she does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If they do not speak after hearing it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
That nun, having been dragged even into the midst of the Saṅgha, should be addressed thus:

"Venerable lady, this monk has been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction; he is disrespectful, unrepentant, and has failed to seek reconciliation."
"Mother, comply with this bhikkhu.
She should be told a second time;
she should be told a third time.
If she relinquishes it, that is well.
If she does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
That bhikkhunī is to be formally admonished.
And furthermore, monks, they should be admonished in this way:
An experienced and competent nun should inform the Saṅgha:
"Let the noble Saṅgha hear me.

This nun, [name], follows a monk who has been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction—[a monk] who is disrespectful, unrepentant, and without an ally—and she does not relinquish that course of action.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha formally admonish the nun [name] so that she may relinquish that course of action.
This is the motion.
"Venerable ladies, let the Saṅgha hear me.

This bhikkhunī, so-and-so, follows a bhikkhu who has been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction— one who is disrespectful, unrepentant, and who has not made amends—
and she does not relinquish that course of action."
The Saṅgha exhorts the bhikkhunī named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter.
Whichever noble lady approves of the exhortation of the bhikkhunī named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter, let her be silent;
whichever does not approve, let her speak.
A second time I speak this matter...
A third time I speak this matter...
The Saṅgha has formally admonished the bhikkhunī named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter.
“The Saṅgha consents, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.
There is an offense of wrong-doing for the motion, and offenses of grave misconduct for the two proclamations.
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
The phrase "this too" is said with reference to the preceding [offenses].
"She becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense" means:

just as a common stone, once split in two, cannot be joined back together, even so a bhikkhunī who does not relinquish [her position] after being formally admonished up to the third time becomes no longer a *samaṇī*, no longer a daughter of the Sakyans. Therefore, she is said to have become one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
"Non-residence":
residence means performing formal acts together, reciting the scriptures together, and training under the same rules.
This is what is meant by "residence. That [residence] does not exist with her; therefore it is called "non-residence."
If it is a legitimate legal act and she perceives it as such, yet does not relinquish her position, there is an offense entailing defeat.
If it is a legitimate legal act but she is unsure of it, yet does not relinquish her position, there is an offense entailing defeat.
If it is a legitimate legal act but she perceives it as an illegitimate legal act, yet does not relinquish her position, there is an offense entailing defeat.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as a legitimate legal procedure, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one is doubtful about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as an illegitimate legal procedure, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense for one who does not admonish,
or for one who relinquishes [the matter].
...for one who is insane ...pe...
for one who is a first-offender.
The third Pārājika is finished.
